original_value: Due to the short range of the sensor technology used in automated vehicles, we assume that the implemented driving strategies may initially differ from those of human drivers. Nevertheless, automated vehicles must be able to move safely through manual road traffic. Initially, they will behave as carefully as human learners do. In the same way that driving-school vehicles tend to be marked in Germany, markings for automated vehicles could also prove advantageous. To this end, a simulation study with 40 participants was conducted. All participants experienced three different highway scenarios, each with and without a marked automated vehicle. One scenario was based around some roadworks, the next scenario was a traffic jam, and the last scenario involved a lane change. Common to all scenarios was that the automated vehicles strictly adhered to German highway regulations, and therefore moved in road traffic somewhat differently to human drivers. After each trial, we asked participants to rate how appropriate and disturbing the automated vehicle’s driving behavior was. We also measured objective data, such as the time of a lane change and the time headway. The results show no differences for the subjective and objective data regarding the marking of an automated vehicle. Reasons for this might be that the driving behavior itself is sufficiently informative for humans to recognize an automated vehicle. In addition, participants experienced the automated vehicle’s driving behavior for the first time, and it is reasonable to assume that an adjustment of the humans’ driving behavior would take place in the event of repeated encounters.

result.paraphrase: Because the sensor technology used in automated vehicles has a limited range, we assume that the implemented driving strategies may initially differ from those of human drivers. Even so, automated vehicles must be capable of moving safely in mixed traffic with manual road users. At first, they will behave as cautiously as learner drivers. As driving-school vehicles are commonly marked in Germany, markings for automated vehicles may also be beneficial. To investigate this, we conducted a simulation study with 40 participants. Each participant experienced three highway scenarios, each once with and once without a marked automated vehicle. The scenarios involved roadworks, a traffic jam, and a lane change. In every case, the automated vehicles strictly followed German highway regulations and therefore behaved somewhat differently in traffic than human drivers. After each trial, participants rated how appropriate and how disturbing the vehicle’s driving behavior was. We also recorded objective measures such as lane-change time and time headway. The findings showed no differences in either subjective or objective data with regard to marking the automated vehicle. This may be because the driving behavior itself is sufficiently informative for people to recognize an automated vehicle. Moreover, participants encountered the automated vehicle’s behavior for the first time, and it is reasonable to assume that humans would adjust their driving behavior after repeated encounters.
